strengths: The composed person retrieval setting is useful and well motivated. ITCPR provides a potentially valuable benchmark with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets; manually checking additional relevant images is a positive design choice.

The two-stage approach is technically plausible and clearly illustrated. Domain-specific encoder fine-tuning followed by lightweight textual inversion enables composed retrieval without training on annotated CPR triplets.

The reported improvements over simple fusion are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.913% Rank-1 and 55.630% mAP, versus 32.016% and 41.831% for image–text feature averaging using the fine-tuned encoders.

Experiments cover two backbones, visual versus textual supervision, training-data volume, network architecture, token length, and ensembling. Training hyperparameters and runtime measurements provide useful practical information.
weaknesses: The central comparison with prior textual-inversion methods is confounded. Table I explicitly states that the Pic2Word and SEARLE inversion networks were trained with the original CLIP parameters, even when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This can introduce representation mismatch. Retraining these baselines with the same adapted encoders and comparable person data is essential. Since Word4Per largely combines an existing pseudo-token pipeline with established alignment losses, this missing control substantially weakens the evidence for its methodological contribution.

The model-selection protocol is unclear. ITCPR is described as exclusively for testing, yet its results guide architecture and template choices in Figure 7 and Table V; no separate validation procedure is specified. This creates a risk of test-set tuning. Repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are also absent, making small differences between supervision and ensemble variants difficult to interpret. These evaluation concerns are the main reasons for the rejection recommendation.

Benchmark reliability needs stronger documentation. The false-negative correction procedure uses retrieved top-k candidates, but the encoder, retrieval depth, annotation agreement, and residual-error audit are unspecified. This procedure does not establish exhaustive relevance labeling. Results broken down by source dataset and clothing-change severity would also help determine whether aggregate performance reflects robust identity-preserving composition.

The proposed explanation that textual supervision suppresses background information is suggestive rather than established. Figure 9 examines the shared frozen visual encoder, not the information retained by different inversion networks. The few self-retrieval examples in Figure 10 cannot distinguish background suppression from reduced reconstruction fidelity; controlled background interventions would provide stronger evidence.

Some implementation descriptions need reconciliation for reproducibility. The aggregation point for multiple TINets is ambiguous, and the text selects template No. 4 in Table V while the inference description and main reported configuration correspond to No. 5. These are fixable issues, but the exact evaluated configuration should be unambiguous.

The manuscript does not document source-data licenses or permissions for the proposed dataset redistribution, or discuss privacy implications and misuse of identifying people across clothing changes. Public availability of the source datasets does not resolve these questions; the intended person-tracking application warrants a concrete ethics discussion.
